title: ‘Master manipulator’ police officer should not be released early from UK prison, says ex-partner
text:
A woman who was coercively controlled by her “master manipulator” partner, who was a police officer, says she is frightened and angry to have learned he will be released early after serving just a third of his sentence.
Michael Harvey worked as a detective in Lancashire police’s sexual offenders management unit when he met Catherine Dobson, using the police database to track her movements after a chance encounter in a supermarket.
She thinks police officers who have abused their position to target women and girls should not be eligible for the government’s early release programme. The charity Women’s Aid has said it believes as many as 5,000 women like her could be affected by the early release of abusive partners.
Dobson worked for the BBC in Salford at the time of her relationship with Harvey. She was one of the keepers of the famous Blue Peter badges, dishing them out to deserving viewers.
She first encountered Harvey while shopping in Asda in Rawtenstall, east Lancashire, in May 2012. He told her she had made his day with her “beautiful smile”.
Six months later she bumped into him again at the same Asda. He greeted her with the words: “Hello stranger, I let you walk away last time and I’ve been kicking myself ever since.” They got chatting and he told her he was a detective, before asking her out for a drink.
She wasn’t looking for a relationship but says she threw caution to the wind after hearing about his job, “because he’s looking after vulnerable women and children every day of his working life”. He told her he was separated from his wife, with whom he shared three children.
It was the first of a series of increasingly outlandish lies he told to lure her in, and then keep her in what quickly became a dysfunctional relationship.
Every time she tried to leave him, he told her something new and devastating: that he had been abused as a child; that he had PTSD after being drafted in to identify body parts in Sri Lanka after the 2004 tsunami; that he had a rare cancer.
In court, he admitted none of that was true.
Dobson also learned that the second meeting in Asda had not been a coincidence at all. Harvey admitted misusing the police database by looking her up five times after their first encounter. He had also looked up her insurance, to see if there was a male driver listed.
After Harvey was sentenced to 30 months in jail, Lancashire police described him as a “master manipulator who used empty threats and emotional blackmail to launch a calculated campaign of control over the victim”.
The emotional blackmail included repeated threats to kill himself if Dobson finished the relationship. “One day we were sitting on my stairs in the hallway and he looked up and he said: ‘I know how much rope I need to hang myself from your loft hatch,’” she recalled.
By September 2015, she discovered he had been messaging women on his work phone. “When I challenged him, he’d said they were victims of sexual abuse and that he was an investigating officer and he was supporting them,” said Dobson. But the messages were deeply inappropriate: “One of the women, he told her she was fit and he was going to take her out for dinner. And when I challenged him, he said, well, yes, but her self-esteem is so low. The abuse was so bad. She just needs lifting up.”
Years later, she reported him for the abuse. In February he was sentenced to 30 months in jail after pleading guilty to coercive and controlling behaviour and misuse of the police database.
Sentencing him, the judge said he had “caused significant psychological harm and very serious distress”, adding: “The public need to see the courts punish police officers who betray public confidence and trust and fall short of the high standards expected of them. In the words of your victim, quote, you were a charming detective on a sex offenders unit paid to protect her from men like you.”
Harvey was found not guilty of raping Dobson three times during the period when she said she was finally trying to leave him.
At the sentencing hearing, a stranger introduced herself to Dobson, saying she, too, had been in an abusive relationship with Harvey. She had been preparing to give evidence against him but was not called after he pleaded guilty to coercive control.
Both women were appalled to learn that Harvey would be released at the end of November after serving just a third of his sentence, as part of the government’s early release scheme.
“I’m angry. Frightened,” said Dobson. “It’s almost like I’ve put myself through the justice system for nothing.”
She said she had agreed when Andy Burnham changed the rules of early release so that the killers of the police officer Andrew Harper would not be eligible. “But he exception should also apply to serving police officers who have chosen to commit heinous crimes,” she said.
Noting that the Ministry of Justice has launched an investigation into whether Russell Brand has broken prison rules, after the jailed comedian shared a message claiming he was not guilty of sexual offences, Dobson said: “If they can have an emergency meeting about Russell Brand they can have an emergency meeting about serving police officers in jail for abusing women.”
